reason: THE BOUND: I looked for any compiler behaviour, defective ones included, that makes GR3 false while the TERM half of the determination stands (every character position is a natural boundary). There is none. Every elementary item at 1985 occupies whole character positions (the 1985 standard has no bit-level data), so whatever position it begins at is the left character position of a one-character boundary. I tried: slack before or after the item, an item inflated to a wider slot with its value at the other end, an overlap of a neighbour, an item kept outside the record so REDEFINES sees stale bytes, and per-occurrence slack under OCCURS. Each one breaks GR1, GR5, the record layout or the BEHAVIOUR half of DOC-A.1-197 ('performs no positioning, adds no slack bytes'), never GR3. Run s13lr-002 (mine) found no slack anywhere at --std 85 and a 15-byte file record. THE TERM: the 1985 text does not leave the meaning of natural boundary wholly free. It ties natural boundaries to 'the computer memory' (VI.5.13.1) and names byte boundaries among them (IV.4.3.7). It leaves to the implementor which boundary is appropriate for an item (GR8b), the placement under bare SYNC (GR2) and the hardware (GR8 'This clause is hardware dependent'). A byte-addressed target with byte boundaries chosen as the appropriate ones is inside that latitude. THE DETERMINATION: quoted truly. DOC-A.1-197 says 'WiseOwl COBOL treats every byte position as a natural boundary'. Its words 'The same in every edition.' follow the example sentence, so they are best read as covering the entry, not proved to. At 1985 a character position is one byte (no national data), so 'byte' and 'character' agree there.
